newsitem.title: USA: Newt Gingrich - once all powerful, now demonized.
newsitem.headline: Newt Gingrich - once all powerful, now demonized.

text.p: Two years ago Newt Gingrich ruled Washington like a king, his every word dissected as the prophet of the Republican revolution in Congress.

Now, with just weeks to go before the Nov. 5 election the speaker of the House of Representatives has faded, demonised by Democrats and held at arm's length even by some Republicans fearful of losing the congressional majority they won in 1994.
Democrats are counting on Gingrich's woes to boost their chances of not only sweeping Bill Clinton back to the White House, but returning Democratic majorities to Congress.

The reason? Polls show Gingrich is one of the most unpopular politicians in America. In a July Washington Post-ABC poll 54 percent called him "too extreme" and 63 percent said he put politics ahead of the national good.

Reuter pollster John Zogby said suburban women were particularly unhappy with the Republican revolution, which many of them think has failed to address such close-to-home issues as childcare for working mothers.
"Newt Gingrich is the lightning rod," he said.

It is a far cry from the heady days of 1995 when Gingrich led House Republicans on a 100-day sprint toward completion of their policy manifesto called the "Contract with America" and Clinton was forced to declare himself still "relevant."

The speaker's unpopularity traces back most notoriously to his declaration in 1995 that he helped close the government because he was snubbed by Clinton on a foreign trip. The New York Daily News pounced on that, portraying the speaker as a child in a front-page cartoon headlined "Cry Baby."

Republicans took most of the blame for two highly unpopular government shutdowns because of a bitter dispute with Clinotn over balancing the budget, polls show. Democrats have also filed ethics charges against the speaker.

Gingrich, acknowledging he has been tarnished by such charges and blaming an unfriendly press, said in an interview published this week in the Washington Times that it may take him 20 years to regain his reputation.

In an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Gingrich said his people had cooperated "totally" with the independent counsel investigating the ethics charges and he favoured releasing the counsel's report once it was finished.
"I'm not delaying anything," he said, adding that of the 66 charges filed by Democrats, "65 are gone."
Tony Blankley, the speaker's press secretary and adviser, said opponents have demonised Gingrich. The Democrats are not about to stop.
"Gingrich will be a target, no doubt about it," said Jim Whitney of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. "Newt will be a major part of these campaigns."
The AFL-CIO labour federation has run ads on more than 150 television stations blaming Gingrich for trying to cut back Medicare, and naming Republican congressmen as his helpers.

For all that, those who work with Gingrich say he is a help, not a hindrance, to Republican candidates. Rich Galen, communications director for Gingrich's political office, said the speaker was going into districts at the request of Republican candidates.
"We have more requests for him to visit than we have time," said Galen, adding that in August alone Gingrich visited 11 congressional districts even with time off for the Republican convention.

But political analysts and even some members of Congress say that not everyone welcomes the speaker. A Republican member of Congress, who asked not to be identified, said of many of his colleagues: "They're worried about being linked to Newt Gingrich."
J.D. Hayworth, a freshman Republican from Arizona who is considered vulnerable to defeat in November, appears to be distancing himself from Gingrich.
"My job is to work for the people of the Sixth District of Arizona," he said. "That is on a separate spot on the ballot from the president. And Newt Gingrich isn't on the ballot."

Even Rick White, a Washington State freshman who invited Gingrich into his district for a fundraiser and press conference in August, is careful to say he makes up his mind independently rather than voting blindly with the leadership.
